title: Liquid IV vs Pedialyte for a Hangover: Which Is Better?
excerpt: Liquid I.V. or Pedialyte after a night out? How their sodium, potassium, and sugar really compare, which to pick if you have been vomiting, and what neither one can fix.
metaDescription: Liquid IV vs Pedialyte for a hangover: how their sodium, potassium, and sugar compare, which to pick when you have been vomiting, and what neither can fix.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** when you mix them the way the labels say, Liquid I.V. and Pedialyte Classic end up surprisingly similar. Per liter of finished drink, they carry about the same amount of sodium, about the same amount of potassium, and a similar amount of sugar. The real differences are in the serving size, the type of sugar, the extra vitamins in Liquid I.V., the format (powder stick versus ready-to-drink bottle), the taste, and the price. For an ordinary hangover, either one is a reasonable way to rehydrate, and neither one is a hangover cure. If you've been vomiting or have diarrhea, Pedialyte (especially its higher-sodium versions) is built closer to a medical rehydration drink and is the safer pick. If you just want something portable and pleasant to drink the morning after, Liquid I.V. is fine.

**The quick rules:** Pick Pedialyte if you've been throwing up, have diarrhea, want less added sugar, or are buying for a child (and in that case, call your pediatrician). Pick Liquid I.V. if you want a stick you can carry in a pocket, you like the taste better, and you don't mind about 11 grams of sugar per stick. Either way, mix it with the full amount of water the label says, sip it over 30 to 60 minutes rather than chugging it, and don't stack several servings on top of a salty breakfast.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label information. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor before using electrolyte drinks regularly if** you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or diabetes, you've been told to limit salt or fluids, or you take medicines that affect sodium or potassium (some blood pressure pills and water pills, for example). **Get medical help if** you can't keep any fluids down for more than about a day, you have signs of significant dehydration (dizziness or fainting when you stand, confusion, very dark urine, or little or no urination), you see blood in vomit or stool, or you have chest pain or a racing heart that doesn't settle. **Call 911** if someone who has been drinking can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin.

## Liquid I.V. vs Pedialyte at a Glance

Here's how the two most common versions compare. Numbers are approximate and based on the original Liquid I.V. Hydration Multiplier and Pedialyte Classic. Formulas change and flavors vary, so check the label on the product you actually buy.

| | Liquid I.V. Hydration Multiplier (original) | Pedialyte Classic (ready-to-drink) |
|---|---|---|
| Format | Powder stick, mix with 16 oz of water | Ready-to-drink liquid (powder packs also sold) |
| Serving used here | 1 stick in 16 oz (about half a liter) | 12 oz (about 355 ml) |
| Sodium per serving | About 500 mg | About 370 mg |
| Potassium per serving | About 370 mg | About 280 mg |
| Sugar per serving | About 11 g (cane sugar and dextrose) | About 9 g (dextrose) |
| Sodium per liter of finished drink | Roughly 1,000 mg | Roughly 1,035 mg |
| Extras | Vitamin C and several B vitamins | Chloride, zinc in some versions; no vitamin focus |
| Designed for | General hydration, marketed to adults | Rehydration during illness, labeled for kids and adults |
| Easy to carry | Yes, very | Bottles are bulky; powder packs travel well |

The row people usually skip is the most important one. Liquid I.V. looks saltier per serving, but that's partly because its serving is bigger. Spread across a liter of finished drink, the two land within a few percent of each other on sodium.

## Is Liquid I.V. the Same as Pedialyte?

Not exactly, but they're closer cousins than the marketing suggests. Both are based on the same idea, which medicine figured out decades ago: your small intestine absorbs water fastest when sodium and glucose arrive together, because they share a transport system in the gut wall. Water follows them in. This is the principle behind oral rehydration solutions (ORS), the simple salt-and-sugar drinks the World Health Organization uses to treat dehydration from diarrhea around the world.

Pedialyte was built as a retail version of that idea. It came out of the medical world as a drink for children with vomiting and diarrhea, and its sodium, potassium, and glucose are set in a ratio close to medical guidance for mild dehydration. Liquid I.V. took the same science, called it "Cellular Transport Technology," added vitamins and more flavor, and sold it as an everyday hydration product for adults.

So the core engine is the same. What differs is everything around it.

### Where they really differ

- **Type of sugar.** Pedialyte Classic uses dextrose, which is glucose. Liquid I.V. uses a mix of cane sugar and dextrose. Cane sugar (sucrose) splits into half glucose and half fructose in your gut. Only the glucose part drives the sodium-glucose transport system, so gram for gram, a bit less of Liquid I.V.'s sugar is doing the rehydration work. In practice, for a hangover, this is a small difference.
- **Total sugar you actually drink.** If you drink one stick of Liquid I.V., you get about 11 grams of sugar. Many people drink two or three on a bad morning, which adds up to 22 to 33 grams, close to a can of soda. Pedialyte Classic has about 9 grams in a 12-ounce glass, and its sugar-free and "lite" versions have less.
- **Vitamins.** Liquid I.V. adds vitamin C and several B vitamins. There's no good evidence that these extra vitamins make a hangover better. Most people who eat a normal diet aren't short on them, and your body passes extra water-soluble vitamins in urine.
- **Format and convenience.** A Liquid I.V. stick weighs almost nothing and fits in a wallet. A liter bottle of Pedialyte doesn't. If you want something in your bag for a wedding or a trip, that matters. Pedialyte does sell powder packs too, which close most of that gap.
- **Taste.** This is personal, but it's the reason a lot of people choose one over the other. Pedialyte Classic tastes salty and slightly medicinal to many adults. Liquid I.V. is sweeter and more like a flavored drink. The drink you'll actually finish beats the "better" drink you'll leave half full.
- **Medical positioning.** Pedialyte is labeled for use in children and comes with age-based guidance. Liquid I.V. is marketed to adults. If a child is sick, call your pediatrician rather than reaching for either one on your own.

## Which Is Better for a Hangover: Liquid I.V. or Pedialyte?

For a typical hangover, where you drank more than you meant to, slept badly, and woke up with a dry mouth and a headache, **neither one has a clear advantage**. Both replace water and some sodium and potassium. Both will help you feel less parched faster than plain water alone, mostly because you're more likely to drink enough of a flavored drink and because the salt helps you hold on to the fluid.

Where they split apart is when your situation isn't typical.

### Pedialyte is the better pick if...

- **You've been vomiting or have diarrhea.** These cause much bigger losses of water and electrolytes than drinking alone. Pedialyte's lower sugar and medical-style formula make it the gentler choice, and the higher-sodium **Pedialyte AdvancedCare Plus** and **Pedialyte Electrolyte Solution** versions are built for bigger fluid losses. Check the label for the exact sodium level, since it varies by version.
- **Your stomach is upset.** Very sweet drinks can be harder to keep down when you're nauseous, and too much sugar in the gut can pull water the wrong way and loosen stools. Small sips of a less sweet drink usually go down better. Our guide to [hangover nausea](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has more on calming a queasy stomach.
- **You're watching sugar**, for example if you have diabetes or prediabetes. Pedialyte's sugar-free options are easier to fit in, though you should still check with your doctor about which is right for you.
- **You want a ready-to-drink option.** Opening a cold bottle is easier than mixing a powder when you feel awful.

### Liquid I.V. is the better pick if...

- **You want to carry it with you.** A couple of sticks in a pocket means you can mix one before bed after a night out, or first thing the next morning, wherever you are.
- **You like the taste more.** If Pedialyte is a struggle to drink, the better-tasting option wins.
- **You want the extra vitamins anyway.** They won't fix a hangover, but if you like the idea of a little vitamin C and B vitamins, Liquid I.V. includes them.

For a deeper look at the Liquid I.V. side alone, including timing and how many sticks make sense, see our guide on [Liquid I.V. for a hangover](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-for-hangover).

## What Electrolyte Drinks Can and Can't Do for a Hangover

This part is easy to miss in product comparisons, so it's worth being clear about.

### What they help with

Alcohol makes you pee more. It does this by suppressing a hormone called vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of that signal, more water leaves your body. Add a warm bar, dancing, sweating, and maybe vomiting, and you can wake up genuinely short on fluid.

That fluid shortfall contributes to a few classic hangover symptoms:

- Thirst and a dry mouth
- Feeling lightheaded, especially when you stand up
- Part of the headache for some people
- Dark urine

An electrolyte drink helps with these by putting water back and helping your body keep it. That's a real benefit, and it's the honest case for both products.

### What they don't fix

Researchers who study hangovers, including the international Alcohol Hangover Research Group, have found that dehydration doesn't explain most of how bad a hangover feels. In studies comparing people's blood electrolyte and hormone levels with how hungover they say they are, the numbers line up poorly. Much of the misery seems to come from other things:

- **Inflammation.** Heavy drinking triggers an immune response that can leave you feeling achy, foggy, and unwell.
- **Acetaldehyde.** This is a toxic chemical your liver makes while it breaks alcohol down. It builds up when you drink faster than your body can clear it.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol may help you fall asleep, but it breaks up the second half of the night. A lot of the next-day exhaustion is plain sleep loss.
- **Low blood sugar and stomach irritation**, which add to the shaky, queasy feeling.

No electrolyte drink addresses those. So if you rehydrate fully and still feel terrible, that's expected, not a sign you picked the wrong brand. There is no good evidence that Liquid I.V., Pedialyte, or any electrolyte drink prevents a hangover or shortens one beyond helping with the dehydration part.

## The Numbers: Sodium, Potassium, and Sugar Side by Side

If you like to understand what you're drinking, here's the per-liter math in plain terms.

**Sodium.** Pedialyte Classic contains about 45 milliequivalents of sodium per liter, which is roughly 1,035 mg. One Liquid I.V. stick (about 500 mg of sodium) mixed into 16 ounces of water works out to roughly 1,000 to 1,050 mg per liter. So the two are essentially the same saltiness when mixed as directed. For comparison, the WHO's reduced-osmolarity oral rehydration solution, which is made for real illness rather than a hangover, has about 75 millimoles of sodium per liter, noticeably saltier than either.

**Potassium.** Pedialyte Classic has about 20 milliequivalents of potassium per liter, roughly 780 mg. Liquid I.V. at 370 mg per 16 ounces works out to about the same per liter. Again, very close.

**Sugar.** Pedialyte Classic has about 25 grams of dextrose per liter. Liquid I.V. at 11 grams per 16 ounces is about 23 grams per liter. Close in amount, different in type, as explained above.

**Calories.** Both are low. A stick of Liquid I.V. is roughly 45 calories. A 12-ounce glass of Pedialyte Classic is around 35.

What this tells you: **the biggest variable isn't the brand, it's how you mix and how much you drink.** If you put a Liquid I.V. stick into 8 ounces of water instead of 16, you've made a drink twice as salty and twice as sweet as intended. If you drink three servings of either, you've tripled everything.

## How to Use Either One After a Night Out

A few habits make a bigger difference than which box you buy.

1. **Mix it as directed.** Liquid I.V. goes into 16 ounces of water. Pedialyte powder packs have their own water amount on the box. Don't make it stronger to "work faster." A drink that's too concentrated can actually slow absorption and upset your stomach.
2. **Sip, don't chug.** Drink it over 30 to 60 minutes. Gulping a big volume on a queasy stomach is a good way to bring it back up.
3. **One serving, then plain water.** For most hangovers, one serving followed by regular water and a meal is plenty. Food brings its own sodium and potassium.
4. **Watch the sodium total.** One Liquid I.V. stick has about 500 mg of sodium. US dietary guidelines suggest most adults stay under about 2,300 mg a day. Two or three sticks plus a bacon-egg-and-cheese breakfast can put you past that by lunch.
5. **Before bed can help too.** Some people mix a serving before going to sleep after drinking. That's a reasonable habit, since you're starting the fluid catch-up earlier. Our guide on [whether to take electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) goes through the timing in more detail.
6. **Eat something.** Toast, eggs, bananas, soup, or rice are all easy on the stomach and help stabilize blood sugar.

If you want the full step-by-step on getting fluids back efficiently, see our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking).

## Cost: Which Gives You More for Your Money?

Prices change often and vary by store and pack size, so treat this as a general guide and compare current prices yourself.

- **Liquid I.V.** is usually sold in boxes of sticks. Per serving, it tends to cost more than a liter of store-brand oral rehydration solution, but you're paying for convenience and flavor.
- **Pedialyte** in liter bottles is usually more expensive per liter than its powder packs. Store-brand electrolyte solutions with the same basic formula are often noticeably cheaper than either name brand.
- **The cheapest option of all** is making your own. A basic homemade drink with water, a little salt, and a little sugar or juice follows the same sodium-glucose principle. Our [homemade electrolyte drink](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) guide gives a simple recipe and the measurements that matter, since too much salt is the most common mistake.

If you're only buying for an occasional hangover, the price difference over a year is small. Buy whichever one you'll actually drink.

## How Do They Compare With Other Options?

Liquid I.V. and Pedialyte aren't the only choices, and sometimes they're not the best ones.

- **Plain water** fixes most of a mild hangover's fluid shortfall, especially with a meal. It's free and has no sugar. It just doesn't replace electrolytes on its own.
- **Gatorade and other sports drinks** have less sodium and more sugar than either Liquid I.V. or Pedialyte. They're fine if that's what you have, but they're designed for athletes. Our [Pedialyte vs Gatorade](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) comparison breaks down the difference.
- **LMNT** has about twice the sodium of Liquid I.V. and no sugar. It suits heavy sweaters and low-carb eaters but can be too salty for some people the morning after. See [LMNT vs Liquid I.V.](/never-hungover/lmnt-vs-liquid-iv) for the details.
- **Electrolit** is another ready-to-drink oral rehydration drink, popular in Mexico and increasingly in the US, with a sodium level in a similar range to Pedialyte. Our [Electrolit vs Pedialyte](/never-hungover/electrolit-vs-pedialyte) guide compares the two.

- **Gatorlyte** is the sports-drink brand's own rehydration formula, closer to Pedialyte than regular Gatorade. See [Gatorlyte vs Pedialyte](/never-hungover/gatorlyte-vs-pedialyte).

For a broader ranked list, our [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) guide covers the whole field, our [electrolyte drinks for a hangover compared](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) table lines up the main brands side by side, and [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) explains which minerals drinking actually depletes.

## Who Should Be Careful With Either Drink

Both drinks are safe for most healthy adults in normal amounts. But the sodium and potassium in them are real doses, not just flavoring. Check with your doctor before using them regularly if you:

- **Have high blood pressure** or have been told to limit salt
- **Have kidney disease**, since your kidneys are responsible for clearing extra sodium and potassium
- **Have heart failure** or have been told to limit fluids
- **Have diabetes**, because the sugar counts toward your daily carbs (sugar-free versions exist for both brands, but ask what's right for you)
- **Take medicines that raise potassium**, such as some blood pressure drugs (ACE inhibitors and ARBs) or potassium-sparing water pills

For children, don't guess at amounts. Pedialyte has age-based guidance on its label, but for a sick child the right move is to call your pediatrician, who can tell you how much to give based on age and weight.

## When a Hangover Is More Than a Hangover

Most hangovers pass within a day with fluids, food, and rest. But some situations need more than a sports drink or a rehydration solution. Get medical help if:

- You **can't keep any fluids down** for more than about a day, or you keep vomiting after every sip
- You have **signs of significant dehydration**: dizziness or fainting when you stand, confusion, a very fast heartbeat, very dark urine, or little or no urination
- You see **blood in your vomit** (it can look like coffee grounds) or in your stool
- You have **chest pain**, severe abdominal pain, or a racing heart that doesn't settle with rest
- You notice **shaking, sweating, anxiety, or seeing or hearing things** a day or two after you stop drinking, especially if you've been drinking heavily for several days in a row. That can be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover, and it can become dangerous. Don't try to ride it out at home; see a doctor or go to urgent care.

**Call 911** if someone who has been drinking can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and no electrolyte drink helps with that.

## The Part Electrolytes Don't Cover

Since rehydration only handles one slice of a hangover, the most effective things are still the unglamorous ones: drink less, drink slower, eat before and while you drink, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, and give yourself time to sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence behind them.

Some people also add a supplement aimed at the alcohol side of the problem rather than the fluid side. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on the brain's response to alcohol. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own. It also doesn't replace fluids, food, or drinking less. If you want to try it, [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) combines DHM with L-cysteine and electrolytes, and [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a simple, lower-cost option. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- Mixed as directed, Liquid I.V. and Pedialyte Classic have about the **same sodium and potassium per liter** and a similar amount of sugar.
- **Pedialyte** is the better choice if you've been vomiting, have diarrhea, have an upset stomach, want less sugar, or are buying for a child (with your pediatrician's guidance).
- **Liquid I.V.** is the better choice if you want something portable and you prefer the taste.
- Both help with the **dehydration part** of a hangover. Neither one fixes inflammation, poor sleep, or the toxic by-products of alcohol, and there is no good evidence that either prevents a hangover.
- Mix it properly, sip it slowly, stop at one or two servings, and eat something.
- If you can't keep fluids down, show signs of serious dehydration, or notice withdrawal symptoms, get medical help instead of reaching for another drink mix.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Liquid I.V. or Pedialyte better for a hangover?**

For a typical hangover, they work about equally well. Mixed as directed, both have roughly the same sodium and potassium per liter and a similar amount of sugar. Pedialyte is the better pick if you've been vomiting, have diarrhea, or want less sugar. Liquid I.V. is the better pick if you want a portable stick and prefer the taste. Neither one cures a hangover; both only help with the dehydration part.

**Is Liquid I.V. the same as Pedialyte?**

No, but they're based on the same science. Both use sodium and glucose together to help your gut absorb water faster, the principle behind medical oral rehydration solutions. Liquid I.V. adds vitamin C and B vitamins, uses cane sugar plus dextrose, and comes as a powder stick. Pedialyte Classic uses dextrose only, is sold ready-to-drink or as powder, and is labeled for children as well as adults.

**Which has more electrolytes, Liquid I.V. or Pedialyte?**

Per serving, Liquid I.V. has more: about 500 mg of sodium and 370 mg of potassium per stick, versus about 370 mg of sodium and 280 mg of potassium in a 12-ounce glass of Pedialyte Classic. But Liquid I.V.'s serving is bigger (16 ounces). Per liter of finished drink, the two are nearly the same. Pedialyte's AdvancedCare Plus and Electrolyte Solution versions have more sodium than Classic, so check the label.

**Which has more sugar, Liquid I.V. or Pedialyte?**

One Liquid I.V. stick has about 11 grams of sugar. A 12-ounce glass of Pedialyte Classic has about 9 grams. Per liter they're similar, but Pedialyte also sells sugar-free and lower-sugar versions, and so does Liquid I.V. If you drink two or three Liquid I.V. sticks on a rough morning, the sugar adds up to roughly a can of soda.

**Should I drink Liquid I.V. or Pedialyte before bed after drinking?**

One serving before bed is a reasonable habit, since it starts replacing fluid earlier. Mix it with the full amount of water, sip it, and don't overdo it. It won't prevent a hangover by itself, because dehydration is only one part of what makes you feel bad, but it can take the edge off thirst and dry mouth in the morning.

**How many Liquid I.V. or Pedialyte servings can I have in a day?**

For most healthy adults, one or two servings on a hangover day is plenty, followed by plain water and food. Each Liquid I.V. stick has about 500 mg of sodium, and US guidelines suggest most adults keep total sodium under about 2,300 mg a day. If you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or diabetes, ask your doctor before using either one regularly.

**Is Pedialyte or Liquid I.V. better when you're throwing up?**

Pedialyte is usually the safer choice when you've been vomiting or have diarrhea, because it's designed for rehydration during illness and comes in lower-sugar and higher-sodium versions. Take small sips every few minutes rather than big gulps. If you can't keep fluids down for more than about a day, or you see blood or feel very dizzy or confused, get medical care.

**Can kids drink Liquid I.V. or Pedialyte?**

Pedialyte is labeled for children and includes age-based guidance. Liquid I.V. is marketed to adults. For a sick child, the best step is to call your pediatrician, who can tell you which product to use and how much to give based on age and weight.
